correctness.rationale: Cai--Kiah--Nguyen--Yaakobi prove that two distinct equal-length words have two common single-deletion descendants exactly when they are Type-A-confusable: they agree outside one interval and inside it are opposite phases of an alternating word on two symbols. For each edge, the first and last differing positions therefore determine a unique interval of length \(L\ge2\); choose its start in \(n-L+1\) ways, the outside word in \(q^{n-L}\) ways, and the unordered symbol pair in \(\binom q2\) ways. The two phases form one unordered edge, so no additional factor occurs. Summing gives the first formula and a finite geometric-derivative calculation gives the closed form and average degree. Independently, direct deletion-ball enumeration matched the formula for 12 \((q,n)\) cases including binary \(n\le7\), ternary \(n\le4\), and selected quaternary cases; the package checker covers a larger grid.

source_inspections.title: Coding for Sequence Reconstruction for Single Edits
source_inspections.trigger: Exact primary theorem characterizing pairs with two common one-deletion reads.

value.rationale: The graph is the natural confusability object for reconstruction from two distinct deletion reads, and its independent sets are exactly codes avoiding this two-read ambiguity. The theorem gives an all-alphabet, all-length density invariant plus a canonical representation of every edge, providing reusable structural input for extremal, probabilistic, and spectral analysis rather than a small isolated count.
residual_risks: Edge density alone does not determine optimal reconstruction-code size.

final_claim: For the \(q\)-ary length-\(n\) single-deletion channel, join two distinct source words when their distinct one-deletion descendant sets intersect in exactly two words. For every \(q\ge2\) and \(n\ge2\), the number of edges is \[\binom q2\sum_{L=2}^n(n-L+1)q^{n-L}=\frac{q\{1-nq^{n-1}+(n-1)q^n\}}{2(q-1)}.\] Every edge has a unique Type-A alternating-interval representation. Consequently the average degree is \(n-q/(q-1)+q^{1-n}/(q-1)\); in the binary case the edge count is \(1+(n-2)2^{n-1}\).
limitations: Edges are defined by exactly two common distinct one-deletion reads, not merely nonempty confusability.
The theorem counts edges and gives the canonical edge representation but does not determine the graph's independence number, spectrum, or degree sequence.
